Italian, but ey oh, I don't mind Latin getting the credit for it. The non-diminutive form of the word comes from the Latin word spacus, meaning twine. I didn't know that offhand; the Internet just makes it easy to sound smert.

Well the transition from singular to plural - the 'o' ending to 'i' ending - is very Latin. As a Romance language, I kind of expect that Italian would retain some of the weird-ass grammatical rules of the parent language.

Well... no, it's very Italian, but Italian is very Latin, so there's that. Latin singular nominative nouns ending -o are third declension, which changes to -es in the plural, such as homo to homines, ratio to rationes, and pugio to pugiones. Quite a few words have stems that change in Latin, which is why these examples don't simply replace the -o with an -es. In order to predict how a noun declines you generally need to know both the nominative and genitive singular forms of the word. Latin inflection is kind of a mess, but it's an extremely beautiful and linguistically pure mess with pretty much the richest cultural history of any language ever, so although it can be a bit intimidating at first, it's very rewarding to learn. I'm an amateur and I've previously memorized all the most important endings, but I had to look all this stuff up to refresh my memory and make sure I had it all straight. Latin nominative singular nouns ending -o aren't particularly frequent, but first person singular verbs, which is generally the dictionary form in Latin, very very frequently end in -o. But there are other cases that end in -o, so in a sentence or whatever, you generally either need to already know the word and how it declines, or know enough of the other words to be able to infer its case from context or from a general familiarity with what various types of words look like.

21 He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them, he it is that loveth me: and he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father, and I will love him, and will manifest myself to him. - John 14:21 (KJV)

If you truly love Jesus, you will try and keep His commandments, not to get anything from God, but just because you love Him. James tells us that faith without works (of faith) is dead (James 2:26), and you can not truly have faith in Jesus and be saved, unless you want to keep His commandments (Hebrews 5:9). You can not truly love someone, and not want to please them. Jesus told us what to do many times (1 John 3:23), and He took the whole Law of the Old Testament, and made it simple, just to love (John 13:34). We can not truly love others if we have not first loved Jesus, and experienced the “AGAPE” type of God’s love ourselves. Jesus loved us enough to come die for us (John 3:16), proving His love for us. We then must show we love Him, by keeping His commandments.

The word translated “manifest” in this verse, means Jesus will “disclose” Himself to us, and we will know He is real and alive. Serving God is just as simple as loving God, and loving others as ourselves, and it means loving with God’s kind of love. It means that you die to yourself, and put others needs above your own. Also we need to obey, and do, the things that Jesus told us we should do, such as minister the Gospel to others (Matthew 28:19), and do the works that Jesus did, and told us we would do (John 14:12). Show that you love Him, by following all His commands and directions, proving that being a Christian is rewarding, and enjoying the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23). Thank you Lord for loving us so very much.
